Chapter 8: Preventing Relapse—Recognizing Early Warning Signs
Let’s talk about something that’s often overlooked but absolutely essential—how do you keep yourself from slipping back into old patterns once things start to get better?
Even after you’ve made real progress, it’s not uncommon for those old habits and feelings to sneak back in, especially when life throws you a curveball.
The good news? Mindfulness gives you some pretty powerful tools to spot those warning signs before they really take hold.
The first step is getting familiar with your own “relapse signature.”
What does that mean?
Well, everyone has their own set of early signals—a certain way of thinking, feeling, or even behaving that hints things might be heading in the wrong direction.
Maybe you find yourself pulling away from friends, skipping your usual self-care, or slipping back into that harsh, self-critical mindset.
By mapping out these patterns, it gets a whole lot easier to spot them early, before they pick up steam.
So what do you do once you notice those warning signs?
Instead of reacting on autopilot, try meeting them with mindful awareness.
Here are a few ways you can do that:
First, pause and check in with yourself.
Take a moment to notice what’s going on inside—your thoughts, your feelings—without judging them.
Next, re-engage with the activities that support you.
Maybe it’s getting outside for a walk, diving into a creative hobby, or reconnecting with someone who lifts you up.
And don’t hesitate to seek support when you need it.
That could mean reaching out to a therapist, a support group, or just someone you trust.
Here’s something really important to remember—relapse isn’t a sign that you’ve failed.
It’s just a natural part of the healing journey.
Think about it: our physical health isn’t always steady, and our emotional well-being works the same way.
The key is to meet yourself with kindness and curiosity, and use every setback as a chance to grow stronger and wiser.
Some people find it really helpful to create a personal “relapse prevention plan.”
What does that look like?
It might include a list of your early warning signs, strategies for self-care, and reminders of what’s helped you in the past—maybe even a few go-to resources you can lean on.
By approaching relapse with both mindfulness and a little preparation, you’ll find it much easier to handle setbacks, and you’ll gain confidence along the way.
Here are the key points to take with you:
Relapse is a normal part of bouncing back from depression or chronic unhappiness.
Spotting your own warning signs gives you a head start on turning things around.
Supportive activities and reaching out for help are both powerful tools.
And finally, having a relapse prevention plan in place can give you structure—and peace of mind—when things get tough.
